summary: Justin, CEO and co-founder of Ionic Commerce, outlines the company's mission to enable AI agents to participate in the economy, beginning with e-commerce. The core thesis is that for 30 years, the digital world has been built for ads and human consumption, not for agent-driven actions. Current product feeds are static, lack real-time inventory and shipping data, and require agents to bounce between sites, which is inefficient for automated transactions. Ionic's solution has three components. First, a data layer: Ionic partners with hundreds of merchants to access product feeds and uses agentic workflows to enrich that data with editorial reviews and other information agents need for decision-making. This enriched data is available in formats agents prefer, including relational databases, vector stores, and graph databases, accessible via a live API. Second, a transaction layer: once an agent and user make a decision, checkout happens in the same layer via payment tokens, eliminating the need to navigate human-designed UX across multiple sites. Third, a monetization model: rather than charging consumers subscription fees, Ionic leverages merchant willingness to pay for agent-driven customer acquisition. Merchants prefer paying Ionic over Amazon because they gain visibility into data flow, model usage, and ongoing customer relationships. Justin contrasts this with agent demos that buy through Amazon, where merchants lose data and relationship control. The platform currently has millions of AI-native SKUs enabled across hundreds of merchant relationships, is actively hiring, and developers can access documentation at docs.ionic.commerce.com or contact Justin or Owen to get started.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & Mission
sections.summary: Justin introduces Ionic Commerce's mission to help agents interact with the economy, starting with e-commerce, motivated by wanting agents to handle tasks like ordering Ubers, finding gifts, and booking hotels on behalf of users.

sections.title: The Problem: Ads vs Actions
sections.summary: Justin explains that for 30 years the digital world was built for ads, not actions. Current product feeds are static, lack real-time inventory and shipping data, and force agents to bounce between sites, which is inefficient for automated transactions.

sections.title: Data Layer: Enriching Product Feeds
sections.summary: Ionic partners with hundreds of merchants, enriches product feeds using agentic workflows with editorial reviews, and makes data available in agent-friendly formats including relational, vector, and graph databases via a live API.

sections.title: Transaction Layer: In-Line Checkout
sections.summary: Once a decision is made, agents can complete checkout in the same layer using payment tokens, eliminating the need to navigate human-designed UI across multiple sites. Justin demonstrates with a headphone purchase example.

sections.title: Monetization: Merchant-Funded Model
sections.summary: Justin argues consumer subscription models won't scale to mass market. Instead, merchants will pay for agent-driven customer acquisition, preferring Ionic's transparent data flow and relationship control over Amazon's opaque model.

sections.title: Getting Started with Ionic
sections.summary: Ionic has hundreds of merchant relationships, millions of AI-native SKUs, is hiring, and developers can access documentation at docs.ionic.commerce.com or contact Justin or Owen to get started.
